# Integrative Cardiopulmonary and Renal Physiology

## 1. Membrane Excitability and Cardiac Action Potentials

Every excitable cell maintains an asymmetric transmembrane ion distribution driven primarily by the electrogenic Na+/K+-ATPase pump, which extrudes 3 sodium ions for every 2 potassium ions imported per molecule of ATP hydrolysed. At rest, membrane permeability is dominated by inward-rectifier potassium channels, pulling the resting membrane potential close to the potassium equilibrium potential predicted by the Nernst equation. For a typical ventricular myocyte, resting potential sits near -90 mV, whereas pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial node lack a prominent inward-rectifier potassium current and exhibit a less negative maximum diastolic potential around -60 mV. Historical electrophysiology studies developed the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz voltage equation to combine the relative permeabilities of sodium, potassium, and chloride into a single steady-state approximation, a conceptual framework that continues to anchor textbook discussions even when modern patch-clamp work resolves dozens of distinct channel isoforms across atrial, Purkinje, and ventricular regions.

Fast-response action potentials in working ventricular myocytes and Purkinje fibres unfold across five classical phases that link electrical excitation to mechanical systole. Phase 0 represents rapid depolarisation through voltage-gated fast sodium channels (INa), driving membrane potential toward +20 to +30 mV within milliseconds; the maximal upstroke velocity (dV/dt max) governs conduction velocity across gap junctions and declines sharply when partial depolarisation inactivates sodium channels, as occurs during severe hyperkalaemia or myocardial ischaemia. Phase 1 produces a brief early repolarisation notch mediated by transient outward potassium currents (Ito), more prominent in epicardial than endocardial cells, contributing to transmural dispersion of repolarisation. Phase 2 forms the characteristic prolonged plateau lasting 200 to 300 milliseconds, sustained by an inward L-type calcium current (ICa,L) balanced against delayed-rectifier potassium efflux; this plateau establishes a long effective refractory period that prevents tetanic contraction in cardiac muscle and protects rhythmic ventricular filling. Phase 3 completes repolarisation as L-type calcium channels inactivate and rapid and slow delayed-rectifier potassium channels (IKr and IKs) predominate, returning the cell to Phase 4 resting stability.

Slow-response pacemaker potentials in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes operate without fast sodium channels and therefore conduct much more slowly. Phase 4 displays spontaneous diastolic depolarisation generated mainly by the hyperpolarisation-activated funny current (If, carrying mixed sodium and potassium influx) together with decaying potassium conductance and late T-type calcium entry. Once threshold near -40 mV is reached, Phase 0 depolarisation proceeds exclusively through L-type calcium channels, explaining why non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem slow sinoatrial rate and prolong atrioventricular nodal conduction while scarcely altering ventricular Phase 0 upstroke velocity. Phase 3 repolarisation relies on potassium efflux without a distinct plateau phase. Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation accelerates Phase 4 slope via cyclic AMP binding directly to HCN channels and phosphorylating calcium channels, whereas parasympathetic vagal acetylcholine activates M2 muscarinic receptors, opens GIRK potassium channels (IK,ACh), hyperpolarises the maximum diastolic potential, reduces cAMP, and flattens Phase 4 slope to slow heart rate.

Excitation-contraction coupling translates sarcolemmal depolarisation into sarcomere shortening through calcium-induced calcium release. During Phase 2, small quantities of extracellular calcium enter via L-type channels situated in transverse tubules directly opposite ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2) release channels on the junctional sarcoplasmic reticulum. This trigger calcium opens RyR2 channels, releasing a large bolus of stored calcium into the cytosol so free calcium concentration rises from roughly 100 nmol/L at rest to more than 1 µmol/L during systole. Calcium binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin away from actin binding sites so myosin heads cycle cross-bridges using ATP hydrolysis. Relaxation (lusitropy) requires active cytosolic calcium clearance: approximately 70% to 75% is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by SERCA2a, regulated by phospholamban, while the remainder exits across the sarcolemma predominantly via the 3Na+/1Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) and plasma-membrane Ca2+-ATPase. Beta-adrenergic phosphorylation of phospholamban relieves its tonic inhibition of SERCA2a, accelerating diastolic relaxation so the ventricle fills adequately even when heart rate rises sharply. Because cardiac myocytes depend tightly on extracellular trigger calcium, severe hypocalcaemia impairs myocardial contractility, whereas cardiac glycosides inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase, raise intracellular sodium, diminish the driving gradient for NCX calcium extrusion, expand sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium stores, and augment positive inotropy at the expense of delayed afterdepolarisations when intracellular calcium overload supervenes.

In skeletal muscle, by contrast, mechanical coupling between dihydropyridine receptors and RyR1 does not require extracellular calcium influx, and action potentials last only 2 to 5 milliseconds, permitting temporal summation and fused tetanus during repetitive motor neuron firing. Vascular smooth muscle introduces a third architecture devoid of troponin: calcium entering through voltage-gated or receptor-operated channels or released via IP3 binds calmodulin, activating myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) to phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains and initiate tone. Conversely, nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase to elevate cGMP and stimulate myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), relaxing arteriolar tone even when cytosolic calcium changes little. Understanding these three distinct excitation-contraction motifs clarifies why drugs selectively target nodal tissue, working myocardium, or resistance arterioles without producing uniform effects across muscle lineages.

Clinical electrocardiography records the spatial summation of myocardial depolarisation and repolarisation waves across body-surface vectors. Normal sinus rhythm originates in the right atrial sinoatrial node at 60 to 100 beats per minute, traverses atrial myocardium in 80 to 100 milliseconds (P wave), pauses physiologically in the atrioventricular node to yield a PR interval of 120 to 200 milliseconds so atrial contraction completes ventricular filling, and then races down the His-Purkinje system to depolarise both ventricles synchronously in less than 120 milliseconds (QRS complex). The QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation; corrected QT (QTc) values exceeding 450 ms in men or 470 ms in women warn of delayed repolarisation and early afterdepolarisations capable of triggering torsades de pointes, especially in the presence of hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, or IKr-blocking medications. Never administer QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics without checking baseline QTc and correcting serum potassium and magnesium first.

## 2. The Cardiac Cycle, Pressure-Volume Loops, and Frank-Starling Mechanics

Mechanical performance of the left ventricle is best analysed through simultaneous pressure-volume loops and Wiggers timing diagrams across the cardiac cycle. At end-diastole, left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) averages 120 mL and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) sits near 8 to 12 mmHg. Ventricular contraction begins with mitral valve closure (first heart sound, S1), initiating isovolumetric contraction: intraventricular pressure climbs steeply while both mitral and aortic valves remain shut and chamber volume stays constant. Once left ventricular pressure surpasses aortic diastolic pressure (around 80 mmHg), the aortic valve opens and rapid followed by reduced ejection expels approximately 70 mL of blood—the stroke volume—reaching peak systolic pressure near 120 mmHg and leaving an end-systolic volume (LVESV) of roughly 50 mL. Normal left ventricular ejection fraction (EF = SV / LVEDV) therefore ranges from 55% to 70%, and an EF below 40% defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

As ventricular repolarisation begins and wall tension falls below aortic pressure, transient retrograde flow snaps the aortic valve closed (second heart sound, S2, marking the dicrotic notch on the aortic tracing). During isovolumetric relaxation, ventricular pressure plunges rapidly while all four valves remain closed until pressure drops below left atrial pressure, opening the mitral valve. Rapid passive ventricular filling accounts for roughly 75% to 80% of total filling in healthy resting hearts and generates an audible third heart sound (S3) when compliance is overwhelmed by volume overload or systolic failure; passive diastasis follows, and late atrial systole contributes the final 20% to 25% of filling (producing an S4 gallop when an atrium contracts forcefully against a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle, never heard in atrial fibrillation because organised atrial kick is absent). Right-sided chambers follow the same mechanical sequence at far lower pressures—right ventricular systolic pressure normally 15 to 25 mmHg and pulmonary artery diastolic pressure 8 to 12 mmHg—meaning pulmonary valve closure normally lags aortic closure slightly during inspiration as negative intrathoracic pressure augments systemic venous return (physiological splitting of S2).

Stroke volume responds to three primary determinants: preload, afterload, and contractility (inotropy). Preload reflects sarcomere stretch immediately prior to contraction, approximated clinically by end-diastolic volume or, imperfectly when compliance changes, by end-diastolic pressure. The Frank-Starling law states that increasing venous return stretches myocardial fibres toward their optimal actin-myosin overlap length (around 2.2 µm) and increases troponin C calcium sensitivity, raising stroke volume proportionally without requiring neural input. Beyond the flat portion of the curve, however, additional fluid loading fails to increase stroke volume while driving left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure into pulmonary oedema; do not continue aggressive fluid administration once the ventricle operates on the flat limb of the Frank-Starling curve.

Afterload represents the systolic wall stress resisting ventricular ejection, governed by the law of Laplace: wall stress equals intraventricular pressure times chamber radius divided by twice the wall thickness. Concentric ventricular hypertrophy thickens the wall in response to chronic pressure overload (such as aortic stenosis or longstanding hypertension) to normalise systolic wall stress, whereas eccentric hypertrophy dilates chamber radius in volume overload (such as chronic mitral or aortic regurgitation). Acute rises in afterload reduce stroke volume, elevate end-systolic volume, widen the pressure-volume loop vertically, and narrow its horizontal width; conversely, arterial vasodilators shift the arterial elastance line flatter and augment forward stroke volume in failing hearts. Contractility denotes load-independent intrinsic myocardial force generation, represented graphically by the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR, or Ees). Positive inotropes such as dobutamine or epinephrine steepen the ESPVR, shrink end-systolic volume, increase stroke volume, and raise myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO2), whereas negative inotropes, beta-blockers, acidosis, and myocardial ischaemia flatten the ESPVR.

| Mechanical determinant | Pressure-volume loop signature | Primary clinical consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increased preload (LVEDV ↑) | Loop widens to the right; higher SV along same ESPVR | Higher cardiac output until flat Starling limb, then congestion |
| Increased afterload (SVR ↑) | Loop taller and narrower; higher LVESV, lower SV | Acute drop in forward flow; chronic concentric hypertrophy |
| Increased contractility (Ees ↑) | Steeper ESPVR slope; lower LVESV, larger SV | Higher EF and MVO2; risk of ischaemia in CAD |
| Reduced diastolic compliance | Steeper EDPVR curve; higher LVEDP for same LVEDV | Diastolic heart failure (HFpEF), flash pulmonary oedema |

Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume (CO = HR × SV), averaging 5.0 L/min in a resting 70-kg adult (cardiac index 2.5 to 4.0 L/min/m²). Guyton's venous return analysis couples the cardiac function curve with the vascular function curve on a single right-atrial pressure axis. Mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf, normally 7 to 10 mmHg) defines the driving head pushing blood back toward the right atrium against venous resistance. Expanding blood volume or inducing venoconstriction shifts the venous return curve rightward, raising steady-state cardiac output and right atrial pressure; lowering total peripheral resistance rotates the venous return curve steeper upward, amplifying cardiac output provided right atrial pressure does not collapse below atmospheric pressure (the Starling resistor waterfall limit of collapsible venae cavae). During extreme tachycardia above 160 to 180 beats per minute, shortened diastole curtails ventricular filling time and reduces coronary perfusion (which occurs predominantly during diastole in the left ventricle), causing cardiac output to fall despite high heart rate.

Myocardial oxygen balance deserves careful quantitative attention because the left ventricle extracts 65% to 75% of delivered arterial oxygen even at rest, leaving minimal extraction reserve compared with skeletal muscle. Consequently, any increase in myocardial oxygen demand—driven chiefly by heart rate, systolic wall tension, and contractility—must be met almost entirely by proportional increases in coronary blood flow via local metabolic vasodilation (adenosine, nitric oxide, KATP channels). Left ventricular subendocardial perfusion depends on coronary perfusion pressure, approximated as aortic diastolic blood pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (CPP = DBP - LVEDP). When diastolic pressure drops precipitously or LVEDP rises steeply during acute heart failure or tachycardia, subendocardial ischaemia ensues even in the absence of fixed epicardial stenosis.

## 3. Vascular Haemodynamics, Microcirculation, and Starling Forces

Blood flow through the systemic and pulmonary circuits obeys Ohm's hydraulic analogue: flow equals pressure gradient divided by vascular resistance (Q = ΔP / R). Mean arterial pressure (MAP) represents the time-weighted driving pressure perfusing organs across the cardiac cycle, approximated at resting heart rates as diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure (MAP ≈ DBP + 1/3 [SBP - DBP], normal 70 to 100 mmHg). Because systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is defined as (MAP - CVP) / CO × 80 (normal 800 to 1,200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵), arterial pressure depends jointly on cardiac output and arteriolar resistance. Poiseuille's law reveals why small muscular arterioles serve as the dominant resistance vessels: laminar resistance is directly proportional to blood viscosity and vessel length, and inversely proportional to the fourth power of luminal radius (R = 8ηL / πr⁴). Halving an arteriole's radius therefore increases its resistance sixteen-fold, permitting precise regional redistribution of blood flow among skeletal muscle, splanchnic beds, kidneys, and skin without destabilising systemic arterial pressure.

Series and parallel vessel arrangements shape total circulatory resistance differently. Adding resistors in series sums their individual resistances (Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ...), explaining why sequential stenoses along a single artery compound pressure loss. By contrast, systemic organ vascular beds sit in parallel (1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...), meaning total systemic vascular resistance is always lower than the resistance of any single organ bed, and dilating one major parallel circuit—such as active skeletal muscle during endurance exercise or an arteriovenous fistula—drops total systemic vascular resistance substantially unless compensated by sympathetic vasoconstriction elsewhere. Large elastic arteries such as the aorta exhibit high compliance (ΔV/ΔP), storing stroke volume energy during systole and recoiling smoothly during diastole (the Windkessel effect) to maintain continuous forward flow and dampen pulse pressure. With ageing and arteriosclerosis, aortic compliance declines, systolic blood pressure climbs, diastolic blood pressure falls, and pulse pressure widens markedly. Conversely, systemic veins hold roughly 65% to 70% of total blood volume as unstressed and stressed capacitance reservoirs; modest alpha-1 sympathetic venoconstriction mobilises hundreds of millilitres from splanchnic capacitance veins into the central circulation within seconds during haemorrhage or standing.

Turbulent flow disrupts laminar parabolic velocity profiles and generates audible murmurs or bruits whenever the dimensionless Reynolds number (Re = ρvd / η) exceeds roughly 2,000. Elevated flow velocity across a narrowed valve orifice, dilated downstream chamber diameter, or reduced blood viscosity in severe anaemia all raise Reynolds number and produce functional or structural murmurs. Because blood is a non-Newtonian suspension whose apparent viscosity rises steeply as haematocrit climbs above 55% (polycythaemia), extreme erythrocytosis increases resistance and impairs microvascular oxygen transport despite elevated haemoglobin concentration.

Transcapillary fluid exchange across the microvascular endothelium follows the revised Starling equation: net filtration flux equals hydraulic conductivity multiplied by surface area times [(Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi)], where Pc is capillary hydrostatic pressure, Pi is interstitial hydrostatic pressure, πc is plasma oncotic pressure (normally 25 to 28 mmHg, driven chiefly by serum albumin), πi is subglycocalyx/interstitial oncotic pressure, and σ is the endothelial reflection coefficient (close to 1.0 in tight continuous brain capillaries, intermediate in skeletal muscle, and low in hepatic sinusoids). Modern glycocalyx physiology demonstrates that in most non-fenestrated continuous capillaries, the subglycocalyx space maintains low oncotic pressure so modest net filtration occurs along the entire capillary length rather than classical venous-end reabsorption; lymphatic vessels continuously clear this filtered interstitial fluid—roughly 2 to 4 litres per day—back to the thoracic duct and systemic veins. Clinical oedema develops whenever net filtration overwhelms lymphatic drainage through four mechanisms: elevated capillary hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous thrombosis, cirrhosis), reduced plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, hepatic synthetic failure, severe malnutrition), increased endothelial permeability with glycocalyx shedding (sepsis, anaphylaxis, burns), or lymphatic obstruction (filariasis, post-surgical lymphoedema).

Local tissue autoregulation matches microvascular perfusion tightly to metabolic demand across brain, heart, and skeletal muscle. Two complementary mechanisms operate simultaneously: the myogenic response (arteriolar vascular smooth muscle contracts reflexively when transmural stretch rises, stabilising flow across MAP 60 to 150 mmHg in cerebral vessels) and metabolic hyperaemia (accumulating CO2, H+, K+, adenosine, lactate, and local hypoxaemia dilate precapillary arterioles). In the brain, arterial PaCO2 is the most potent physiological modulator of cerebral blood flow across 20 to 80 mmHg: hypercapnia vasodilates cerebral arterioles and elevates intracranial pressure, whereas excessive hyperventilation below PaCO2 25 to 30 mmHg induces cerebral vasoconstriction and risks cerebral ischaemia. Never use prolonged aggressive hyperventilation routinely in traumatic brain injury except briefly as a rescue bridge during impending herniation. In the pulmonary circulation, by contrast, alveolar hypoxia triggers hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV), shunting blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward better-oxygenated lung units—an adaptive local reflex that turns maladaptive into pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale when global hypoxia persists in chronic lung disease or high altitude.

## 4. Autonomic Control and Baroreceptor-Chemoreceptor Reflexes

Short-term arterial blood pressure stability over seconds to minutes relies on the arterial baroreceptor reflex, a negative-feedback loop anchored in stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors within the carotid sinuses (innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX) and the aortic arch (innervated by the vagus nerve, CN X). Afferent impulses project continuously to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the dorsal medulla. When arterial pressure rises, increased vessel stretch accelerates baroreceptor firing rate; the NTS excites the nucleus ambiguus (boosting parasympathetic vagal outflow to the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes) and activates the caudal ventrolateral medulla, which inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM), lowering sympathetic vasoconstrictor and cardiac accelerator tone. Heart rate slows, contractility decreases, arterioles dilate, veins relax, and MAP returns toward its set point.

When arterial pressure falls—for example upon standing abruptly or losing blood volume—baroreceptor stretch and firing rate drop sharply. The NTS withdraws parasympathetic inhibition and disinhibits the RVLM, unleashing sympathetic noradrenergic discharge that elevates heart rate, contractility, arteriolar resistance, and venous return within two heartbeats. Carotid sinus receptors respond to both mean pressure and pulse pressure across a sensitive operating range of roughly 60 to 160 mmHg, whereas aortic arch receptors primarily buffer hypertension and have a higher threshold. Importantly, arterial baroreceptors reset over 24 to 48 hours of sustained hypertension, meaning they defend beat-to-beat stability around a new elevated baseline rather than controlling chronic long-term blood pressure; long-term pressure regulation belongs to the renal pressure-natriuresis mechanism and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

Low-pressure cardiopulmonary mechanoreceptors situated in the atria, right ventricle, and pulmonary veins sense central blood volume rather than arterial pressure. Atrial stretch triggers the Bainbridge reflex (modest heart-rate elevation when venous return surges), inhibits hypothalamic antidiuretic hormone (ADH / arginine vasopressin) release to promote free-water excretion, suppresses renal sympathetic nerve activity, and stimulates atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) secretion. ANP and ventricular brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) bind natriuretic peptide receptor-A to elevate intracellular cGMP, dilate afferent glomerular arterioles while constricting efferent arterioles (raising GFR), inhibit collecting-duct sodium reabsorption, and suppress renin and aldosterone release.

Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (CN IX) and aortic bodies (CN X) monitor arterial PaO2, PaCO2, and pH, responding primarily when PaO2 drops below 60 mmHg (where the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve steepens downward), during acidaemia, or when severe hypoperfusion reduces carotid body oxygen delivery. Unlike central medullary chemoreceptors—which sense cerebrospinal fluid H+ derived from arterial CO2 diffusion and do not respond directly to hypoxaemia—carotid body glomus cells close oxygen-sensitive potassium channels during hypoxia, depolarise, admit calcium, and release neurotransmitters that drive both hyperventilation and sympathetic vasoconstriction. In extreme cerebral hypoperfusion (such as rising intracranial pressure exceeding arterial perfusion pressure), ischaemia of the medullary vasomotor centre triggers the Cushing reflex: intense sympathetic peripheral vasoconstriction drives severe hypertension with widened pulse pressure, followed by baroreceptor-mediated reflex bradycardia and irregular respirations—a late pre-herniation emergency sign.

The autonomic efferent arm divides anatomically and pharmacologically into sympathetic (thoracolumbar T1-L2, short preganglionic cholinergic fibres synapsing on nicotinic NN receptors, long postganglionic noradrenergic fibres except cholinergic sweat glands and direct preganglionic innervation of adrenal chromaffin cells) and parasympathetic (craniosacral CN III, VII, IX, X and S2-S4, long preganglionic fibres, short postganglionic muscarinic fibres) divisions. Cardiovascular adrenergic receptor signalling splits cleanly across G-protein cascades: alpha-1 receptors (Gq → IP3/DAG → ↑Ca2+) constrict vascular smooth muscle and pupillary radial muscle; presynaptic alpha-2 receptors (Gi → ↓cAMP) inhibit further norepinephrine release and reduce central sympathetic outflow; beta-1 receptors (Gs → ↑cAMP) accelerate SA/AV conduction, boost myocardial contractility, and stimulate juxtaglomerular renin secretion; beta-2 receptors (Gs → ↑cAMP) dilate bronchioles and skeletal muscle arterioles, stimulate hepatic glycogenolysis, and drive potassium intracellularly via Na+/K+-ATPase activation.

## 5. Pulmonary Mechanics, Surfactant, Compliance, and Airway Resistance

Ventilation moves air between the atmosphere and gas-exchanging alveoli down bulk pressure gradients generated by respiratory muscles. During quiet inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction flattens the dome downward and external intercostals elevate the ribs in a bucket-handle motion, expanding thoracic volume and making intrapleural pressure more negative—from roughly -5 cmH2O at functional residual capacity (FRC) down to -8 cmH2O. Transpulmonary pressure (PL = Palv - Pip) increases, distending compliant alveoli so intra-alveolar pressure dips to -1 cmH2O and draws in a tidal volume of approximately 500 mL (6 to 8 mL/kg ideal body weight). Quiet expiration is completely passive, driven by inward elastic recoil of lung parenchyma and alveolar surface tension as inspiratory muscles relax, raising alveolar pressure transiently to +1 cmH2O until lung volume settles back at FRC—the equilibrium volume where inward lung elastic recoil exactly balances outward chest-wall spring recoil. Forced expiration recruits internal intercostals and abdominal wall muscles to push pleural pressure positive; in severe obstructive lung disease, dynamic airway compression occurs downstream of the equal pressure point where positive pleural pressure exceeds intraluminal airway pressure in small cartilage-free bronchioles, trapping gas and elevating residual volume.

Lung compliance (CL = ΔV / ΔP) measures static distensibility and depends jointly on parenchymal elastin/collagen architecture and alveolar liquid-air surface tension. According to Laplace's law for a sphere (P = 2T / r), smaller alveoli would suffer higher collapsing pressure than larger alveoli and empty into them if surface tension T remained constant. Type II pneumocytes prevent this instability by secreting pulmonary surfactant—a phospholipid-protein complex rich in dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) and surfactant proteins SP-A through SP-D—beginning around 24 weeks of gestation and reaching functional maturity near 34 to 36 weeks. Surfactant reduces surface tension dramatically and disproportionately more as alveolar radius shrinks during expiration, equalising collapsing pressures across alveoli of different sizes, lowering work of breathing, increasing lung compliance, and keeping alveoli dry by reducing inward capillary fluid pull. Insufficient surfactant causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, whereas surfactant inactivation during acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) triggers diffuse alveolar collapse, stiff non-compliant lungs, and refractory hypoxaemia.

Restrictive and obstructive diseases deform static lung volumes and spirometric flow-volume loops in opposite directions. Static lung volumes divide into four non-overlapping volumes—tidal volume (VT ≈ 500 mL), inspiratory reserve volume (IRV ≈ 3,000 mL), expiratory reserve volume (ERV ≈ 1,100 mL), and residual volume (RV ≈ 1,200 mL)—which combine into four capacities: inspiratory capacity (IC = VT + IRV), vital capacity (VC = IRV + VT + ERV ≈ 4,600 mL), functional residual capacity (FRC = ERV + RV ≈ 2,300 mL), and total lung capacity (TLC = VC + RV ≈ 5,800 mL). Because residual volume cannot be exhaled, neither RV, FRC, nor TLC can be measured by simple spirometry; they require helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or whole-body plethysmography (the latter accurately capturing trapped non-communicating gas pockets in severe emphysema).

| Spirometric / mechanical index | Obstructive (COPD, asthma) | Restrictive (fibrosis, obesity, NMD) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FEV1 / FVC ratio | Reduced (<0.70) | Normal or increased (>0.80) |
| Total lung capacity (TLC) | Normal or increased (hyperinflation) | Reduced (<80% predicted) |
| Residual volume (RV) and FRC | Increased (air trapping) | Reduced (except expiratory muscle weakness) |
| Lung compliance (emphysema vs fibrosis) | Increased in emphysema (loss of elastin) | Decreased in parenchymal fibrosis |
| DLCO | Decreased in emphysema; normal/high in asthma | Decreased in ILD; normal in chest-wall/NMD restriction |

Airway resistance obeys Poiseuille's fourth-power radius relationship, yet counterintuitively the greatest total resistance in healthy lungs resides in medium-sized segmental bronchi (generations 4 to 8) rather than terminal bronchioles. Although each individual terminal bronchiole is tiny, millions arranged in parallel create an enormous combined cross-sectional area with very low total resistance. Consequently, small-airway pathology can advance substantially before altering total airway resistance or FEV1, earning small airways the reputation of the lung's silent zone. Furthermore, airway resistance varies inversely with lung volume because radial traction of surrounding alveolar septa tethers airways open at high lung volumes; patients with acute asthma or emphysema instinctively breathe at elevated FRC to pull narrowed bronchioles open despite the added elastic work of breathing.

Mechanical ventilation physiology applies these principles directly at the bedside. Peak inspiratory pressure (Ppeak) reflects both resistive airway pressure and elastic alveolar distension, whereas plateau pressure (Pplat, measured during an end-inspiratory hold at zero flow) isolates static elastic compliance of the respiratory system. A high Ppeak with a normal Pplat (wide Ppeak - Pplat gradient >5 cmH2O) signals elevated airway resistance—bronchospasm, secretions, kinked endotracheal tube, or biting—whereas elevated Ppeak and elevated Pplat together indicate reduced compliance—ARDS, pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax, auto-PEEP, mainstem intubation, or abdominal compartment syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS strictly limits tidal volume to 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight (never actual body weight in obesity) and keeps plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O with driving pressure (Pplat - PEEP) ideally below 15 cmH2O to avoid barotrauma and volutrauma.

## 6. Gas Exchange, Ventilation-Perfusion Matching, and Oxygen Transport

Alveolar ventilation determines arterial carbon dioxide elimination while matching ventilation to pulmonary capillary perfusion governs arterial oxygenation. Minute ventilation (VE = VT × respiratory rate) includes anatomic dead space (VD ≈ 150 mL, roughly 2 mL/kg) occupying conducting airways where no gas exchange occurs, so only alveolar ventilation (VA = [VT - VD] × RR, normally 4.2 L/min) participates in CO2 clearance. The alveolar ventilation equation establishes an inverse hyperbolic link between alveolar ventilation and arterial PaCO2: PaCO2 is directly proportional to metabolic CO2 production (VCO2) and inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation (PaCO2 = [VCO2 × 0.863] / VA). Doubling alveolar ventilation therefore halves PaCO2, whereas halving alveolar ventilation doubles PaCO2. Physiologic dead space includes both anatomic dead space and alveolar dead space (ventilated alveoli lacking perfusion, as in pulmonary embolism or overdistended West zone 1 lung units), quantified by the Bohr equation: VD / VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2.

Alveolar oxygen partial pressure (PAO2) follows the alveolar gas equation:

$$
P_AO_2 = F_iO_2 \times (P_{\text{atm}} - P_{H_2O}) - \frac{P_aCO_2}{R}
$$

At sea level (Patm = 760 mmHg, PH2O = 47 mmHg, room air FiO2 = 0.21, respiratory quotient R = 0.8, PaCO2 = 40 mmHg), normal PAO2 equals roughly 100 mmHg. Comparing calculated PAO2 with measured arterial PaO2 yields the alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient (normal <10 to 15 mmHg in young adults, rising modestly with age roughly as age/4 + 4). Hypoxaemia with a normal A-a gradient points exclusively to hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen tension (high altitude), whereas an elevated A-a gradient implicates V/Q mismatch, right-to-left shunt, or diffusion impairment. Crucially, hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch or diffusion impairment responds well to 100% supplemental oxygen, whereas a true right-to-left anatomical or intrapulmonary shunt (V/Q = 0, such as hepatopulmonary syndrome, patent foramen ovale with Eisenmenger physiology, or complete alveolar flooding in lobar pneumonia/ARDS) does not normalise PaO2 even on 100% FiO2 because shunted mixed venous blood never contacts alveolar gas.

Gravity creates a vertical gradient of both ventilation and perfusion across upright lungs, classically divided into three West zones. At the lung base (Zone 3, Pa > Pv > PA), hydrostatic weight boosts perfusion far more steeply than ventilation, yielding a lower V/Q ratio (~0.6) yet higher absolute blood flow and gas exchange. At the lung apex (Zone 1 where PA > Pa > Pv only during hypotension or high positive-pressure ventilation; normally Zone 2 where Pa > PA > Pv), ventilation exceeds perfusion (V/Q ~3.0), elevating apical PAO2 (~130 mmHg) and creating a favourable niche for strictly aerobic pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Overall whole-lung V/Q averages 0.8 (VA 4.2 L/min ÷ Q 5.0 L/min).

Diffusion across the 0.3 to 0.5 µm alveolar-capillary barrier follows Fick's law: gas transfer rate is proportional to surface area, diffusion constant (CO2 diffuses roughly 20 times faster than O2 owing to far higher aqueous solubility), and partial pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. In healthy resting lungs, pulmonary capillary blood spends 0.75 seconds traversing an alveolar capillary, yet oxygen equilibrates completely within 0.25 seconds—meaning oxygen transfer is normally perfusion-limited, just like nitrous oxide. During strenuous exercise when capillary transit time compresses toward 0.25 seconds, or in pulmonary fibrosis where membrane thickening slows equilibration, oxygen transfer can become diffusion-limited, precipitating exertional desaturation. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin so avidly that capillary PCO never approaches alveolar PCO; CO uptake is strictly diffusion-limited, making DLCO the clinical yardstick of alveolar-capillary membrane surface area and integrity.

Oxygen travels in arterial blood predominantly bound to haemoglobin (98.5%) and only minimally dissolved in plasma (1.5%). Total arterial oxygen content (CaO2) equals (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2), averaging 20 mL O2 per dL at Hb 15 g/dL, SaO2 98%, and PaO2 95 mmHg. Total systemic oxygen delivery (DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10) averages 1,000 mL/min, of which resting tissues consume roughly 250 mL/min (VO2, normal extraction ratio 25%, mixed venous SvO2 70% to 75%). Cooperative binding among haemoglobin's four haem subunits creates the sigmoidal oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, with normal P50 (PaO2 at 50% saturation) near 27 mmHg. The flat upper plateau (PaO2 60 to 100 mmHg, SaO2 >90%) buffers arterial loading against moderate altitude or mild lung disease, while the steep lower slope facilitates brisk unloading into metabolically active tissues. Factors shifting the curve rightward (higher P50, easier tissue O2 unloading) follow the classic CADET face-right pattern: increased CO2, Acidosis (Bohr effect), elevated 2,3-BPG, Exercise, and elevated Temperature. Conversely, alkalosis, hypothermia, low 2,3-BPG (such as banked red blood cells), fetal haemoglobin (HbF, lacking beta chains to bind 2,3-BPG), and carbon monoxide shift the curve leftward, impairing peripheral O2 release.

Carbon monoxide poisoning binds haem iron with roughly 240-fold greater affinity than oxygen, simultaneously lowering oxygen-carrying capacity and locking remaining haem sites in the high-affinity R state (left shift); standard two-wavelength pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and displays a falsely reassuring SpO2 despite life-threatening cellular hypoxia, requiring co-oximetry and immediate 100% normobaric or hyperbaric oxygen. Methaemoglobinaemia oxidises haem iron from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+), incapable of binding oxygen and shifting remaining sites leftward, producing chocolate-brown blood, fixed SpO2 around 85% refractory to oxygen, and a large saturation gap; treat symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia (>20% to 30% or symptomatic at lower levels) with intravenous methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg (avoid in severe G6PD deficiency because methylene blue requires NADPH to act and can trigger haemolysis). Carbon dioxide returns from tissues to the lungs predominantly as plasma bicarbonate (70%, generated inside erythrocytes by carbonic anhydrase with chloride shift via Band 3 exchanger), carbamino compounds bound to deoxygenated haemoglobin (20% to 23%, enhanced by the Haldane effect), and dissolved CO2 (7% to 10%).

## 7. Control of Breathing, Exercise Integration, and High-Altitude Physiology

Rhythmic spontaneous ventilation originates in the medullary pacemaker network—specifically the pre-Bötzinger complex within the ventral respiratory group—modulated by the dorsal respiratory group (inspiratory integration receiving vagal and glossopharyngeal afferents), the pontine pneumotaxic centre (nucleus parabrachialis, limiting inspiratory duration to increase rate), and the apneustic centre (promoting sustained inspiratory drive). Under physiological conditions at sea level, arterial PaCO2 is the primary minute-to-minute driver of ventilation via central chemoreceptors bathed in cerebrospinal fluid along the ventrolateral medulla. Because the blood-brain barrier is freely permeable to dissolved CO2 yet relatively impermeable to polar H+ and HCO3- ions, rises in arterial PaCO2 rapidly acidify CSF, triggering vigorous increases in tidal volume and respiratory rate. Within 24 to 48 hours of chronic hypercapnia (as in severe COPD), choroid plexus cells transport bicarbonate into CSF to restore CSF pH toward normal, blunting central CO2 responsiveness. In chronically hypercapnic patients, excessive unregulated oxygen therapy can worsen hypercapnia primarily by abolishing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q dead space) and via the Haldane effect (oxygenated haemoglobin releases bound CO2 into blood), alongside modest reduction of hypoxic respiratory drive; target SpO2 88% to 92% in chronic CO2 retainers rather than 100%.

During graded aerobic exercise, cardiopulmonary systems coordinate seamlessly to elevate oxygen uptake ten- to fifteen-fold without altering mean arterial PaO2 or PaCO2 in healthy individuals. Skeletal muscle arteriolar metabolic vasodilation slashes total peripheral resistance while sympathetic venoconstriction and the skeletal muscle pump surge venous return, expanding cardiac output up to 20 to 25 L/min through both heart rate escalation and modest stroke volume augmentation. Pulmonary capillary recruitment and distension drop pulmonary vascular resistance, allowing five-fold higher pulmonary blood flow with minimal rise in pulmonary artery pressure and equalising apical-to-basal V/Q ratios. Mixed venous O2 content drops sharply as working muscle extracts up to 75% to 80% of delivered oxygen, widening the arteriovenous oxygen difference. Minute ventilation rises instantaneously at exercise onset via central motor command and muscle proprioceptor afferents, tracking CO2 production tightly up to the anaerobic threshold, beyond which lactic acidaemia stimulates carotid bodies to drive compensatory hyperventilation and drop PaCO2.

Ascent to high altitude lowers barometric pressure while FiO2 stays fixed at 0.21, decreasing inspired PO2 and arterial PaO2. Once PaO2 drops below 60 mmHg, carotid body chemoreceptors drive hypoxic hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 and creating an acute respiratory alkalosis that initially brakes full ventilatory response until renal bicarbonate excretion over 2 to 5 days compensates pH (accelerated pharmacologically by acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor inducing mild metabolic acidosis). Within hours to days, erythrocyte 2,3-BPG increases to shift the oxyhaemoglobin curve rightward for tissue unloading, while hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α) boosts renal peritubular erythropoietin secretion to expand red blood cell mass over weeks. Global alveolar hypoxia triggers widespread hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, raising pulmonary artery pressure and risking high-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE) or cerebral oedema (HACE) during rapid unacclimatised ascent; descent and supplemental oxygen remain definitive treatment, supplemented by nifedipine for HAPE and dexamethasone for HACE.

## 8. Glomerular Filtration, Autoregulation, and Renal Clearance

Although the kidneys account for less than 0.5% of body mass, they receive 20% to 25% of resting cardiac output—roughly 1,000 to 1,200 mL/min of renal blood flow (RBF) and 600 to 650 mL/min of renal plasma flow (RPF)—principally to sustain a high glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of approximately 120 to 125 mL/min/1.73 m² rather than merely to meet renal metabolic demand. The filtration fraction (FF = GFR / RPF) normally sits near 20%. Filtration crosses a three-layered glomerular barrier: fenestrated capillary endothelium, negatively charged glomerular basement membrane rich in heparan sulphate proteoglycans, and interdigitating podocyte foot processes bridged by nephrin slit diaphragms. This size- and charge-selective sieve freely filters water, electrolytes, glucose, urea, and creatinine while excluding negatively charged plasma proteins such as albumin.

Starling forces govern net glomerular filtration pressure: GFR = Kf × [(PGC - PBS) - (πGC - πBS)], where glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC ≈ 55 to 60 mmHg) favours filtration against Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure (PBS ≈ 15 mmHg) and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (πGC, rising from 25 mmHg at the afferent end to ~35 mmHg at the efferent end as protein-free filtrate leaves), while Bowman's space oncotic pressure (πBS) is normally zero. Manipulating afferent versus efferent arteriolar tone produces predictable, clinically vital shifts in RPF, GFR, and filtration fraction:

| Vascular / pathological change | RPF | GFR | Filtration fraction (GFR / RPF) | Clinical example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Afferent arteriolar constriction | ↓ | ↓ | Unchanged | NSAIDs (block vasodilatory PGE2/PGI2) |
| Afferent arteriolar dilation | ↑ | ↑ | Unchanged | Early diabetes hyperfiltration, ANP |
| Efferent arteriolar constriction | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ | Angiotensin II (low-to-moderate levels) |
| Efferent arteriolar dilation | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | ACE inhibitors / ARBs (lower intraglomerular pressure) |
| Increased Bowman's space pressure (PBS ↑) | Unchanged/↓ | ↓ | ↓ | Ureteral stone, BPH, bilateral obstruction |
| Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (πGC ↓) | Unchanged | ↑ | ↑ | Severe hypoalbuminaemia |

Because ACE inhibitors and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, they lower glomerular hyperfiltration pressure and slow progression of proteinuric diabetic and chronic kidney disease; a modest initial creatinine rise up to 20% to 30% reflects haemodynamic unloading rather than acute tubular injury, whereas abrupt severe AKI after starting an ACE inhibitor flags possible bilateral renal artery stenosis (where efferent angiotensin II constriction was maintaining GFR). Similarly, never combine NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and loop or thiazide diuretics casually in volume-depleted patients—the classic "triple whammy" collapses glomerular filtration by simultaneously constricting the afferent arteriole, dilating the efferent arteriole, and depleting intravascular volume.

Renal autoregulation holds RBF and GFR remarkably stable across mean arterial pressures from 80 to 180 mmHg via two intrarenal mechanisms independent of autonomic nerves. First, the myogenic mechanism constricts afferent arteriolar smooth muscle when elevated systemic pressure stretches the vessel wall. Second, tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) monitors NaCl delivery at the macula densa (specialised thick ascending limb cells abutting the vascular pole): higher GFR increases distal NaCl uptake via NKCC2, triggering macula densa adenosine and ATP release that constricts the adjacent afferent arteriole to pull GFR back down, whereas reduced NaCl delivery suppresses adenosine, releases prostaglandins, and stimulates juxtaglomerular granular cells to secrete renin.

Renal clearance (Cx = [Ux × V] / Px) quantifies the virtual volume of plasma completely cleared of substance X per minute. Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, making inulin clearance the gold standard for GFR. Clinically, serum creatinine approximates GFR inversely, though slight proximal tubular secretion of creatinine overestimates true GFR by 10% to 15% (and drugs like trimethoprim or cimetidine block creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine without lowering true GFR). Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is both freely filtered and ~90% actively secreted by proximal organic anion transporters at low plasma concentrations, so PAH clearance estimates effective renal plasma flow (eRPF), from which RBF = eRPF / (1 - Hct). Comparing clearance ratios reveals net tubular handling: Cx < GFR proves net reabsorption (glucose, amino acids, sodium, urea), whereas Cx > GFR proves net secretion (PAH, potassium under high aldosterone, organic acids).

## 9. Tubular Reabsorption, Countercurrent Multiplication, and Water Balance

Each day the glomeruli filter roughly 180 litres of plasma containing over 25,000 mEq of sodium, yet normal urine output averages only 1 to 2 litres containing less than 1% of filtered sodium—a triumph of segmented nephron transport energised almost everywhere by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) acts as the bulk workhorse, reabsorbing 65% to 70% of filtered sodium, water, and potassium, 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids (via apical SGLT2/SGLT1 sodium-glucose cotransporters until plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold of ~180 to 200 mg/dL and transport maximum Tmax ~375 mg/min), and 85% to 90% of filtered bicarbonate via apical NHE3 Na+/H+ exchange coupled to luminal carbonic anhydrase. Parathyroid hormone inhibits proximal Na+/phosphate cotransporters (NaPi-IIa/c) to cause phosphaturia, while angiotensin II stimulates NHE3 to enhance proximal Na+/HCO3- retention during volume contraction (explaining contraction metabolic alkalosis). Because water follows solute freely through aquaporin-1, tubular fluid leaving the PCT stays iso-osmotic (~300 mOsm/kg). Fanconi syndrome reflects global PCT failure with glycosuria despite normal serum glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and proximal (Type 2) renal tubular acidosis.

The loop of Henle establishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient (300 mOsm/kg in the cortex rising to 1,200 mOsm/kg at the inner medullary papilla) through countercurrent multiplication, preserved by slow hairpin blood flow in the vasa recta acting as a countercurrent exchanger. The thin descending limb is permeable exclusively to water (passively concentrating luminal fluid to 1,200 mOsm/kg as it dives into the hypertonic medulla) and impermeable to sodium. Conversely, the thick ascending limb (TAL)—the diluting segment—is completely impermeable to water while actively reabsorbing 20% to 25% of filtered Na+ via the apical Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2, inhibited by loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide). Back-diffusion of K+ through apical ROMK channels generates a lumen-positive electrical potential (+8 mV) that drives paracellular reabsorption of divalent cations Ca2+ and Mg2+; loop diuretics abolish this lumen-positive voltage and therefore increase urinary calcium and magnesium excretion ("loops lose calcium"). Tubular fluid exiting the TAL is hypo-osmotic (~100 mOsm/kg).

The early distal convoluted tubule (DCT) remains impermeable to water and reabsorbs 5% to 10% of filtered NaCl through the apical Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC, inhibited by thiazide diuretics). Here, PTH directly stimulates apical TRPV5 calcium channels and basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange; thiazides lower intracellular Na+, enhance basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange, and increase calcium reabsorption, reducing urinary calcium excretion and protecting against calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis.

The late distal tubule and collecting duct perform fine hormonal tuning across two specialised cell types. Principal cells reabsorb the remaining 3% to 5% of sodium via apical ENaC channels (blocked by amiloride and triamterene) and secrete potassium into the lumen, generating a lumen-negative potential amplified by aldosterone (which upregulates ENaC, ROMK, and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase). Collecting-duct water permeability is controlled solely by antidiuretic hormone (ADH, released from the posterior pituitary in response to hypothalamic osmoreceptors detecting plasma osmolality >285 mOsm/kg or baroreceptors detecting >10% volume depletion): ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors (Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA) to insert aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, allowing water to equilibrate with the hypertonic medullary interstitium (concentrating urine up to 1,200 mOsm/kg) and also activating inner-medullary urea transporters (UT-A1) to recycle urea and sustain inner medullary hypertonicity. Without ADH, urine remains maximally dilute (~50 mOsm/kg). Alpha-intercalated cells secrete H+ via apical H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase (reabsorbing new bicarbonate via basolateral AE1 Cl-/HCO3- exchange, upregulated by aldosterone) to excrete fixed daily acid loads (~1 mEq/kg/day) buffered by titratable acid (phosphate) and ammonium (NH4+); failure of alpha-intercalated H+ secretion causes distal Type 1 RTA (urine pH >5.5, hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis).

Free-water clearance (CH2O = V - Cosm, where Cosm = [Uosm × V] / Posm) distinguishes water diuresis from antidiuresis: positive CH2O signifies net excretion of solute-free water (low ADH, primary polydipsia, or diabetes insipidus), whereas negative CH2O signifies net water conservation (high ADH, volume depletion, or SIADH). Never correct chronic hyponatraemia (>48 hours duration) faster than 8 mEq/L in any 24-hour period (target 4 to 6 mEq/L in high-risk patients with alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, or severe hypokalaemia) to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome; similarly, avoid overly rapid correction of chronic hypernatraemia (>10 mEq/L per 24 hours) to prevent cerebral oedema.

## 10. Integrated Shock Physiology, Haemorrhage, and Homeostatic Limits

Circulatory shock occurs whenever systemic oxygen delivery (DO2) or cellular oxygen utilisation fails to meet tissue metabolic demand (VO2), forcing cells into anaerobic glycolysis with rising serum lactate (>2 mmol/L). Haemodynamic profiling cleanly separates the four classic shock phenotypes using cardiac output (CO), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP, reflecting left ventricular preload), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2):

| Shock class | Preload (PCWP / CVP) | Pump (CO) | Afterload (SVR) | SvO2 | Prototypes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Hypovolaemic** | ↓ | ↓ | ↑ (compensatory) | ↓ | Haemorrhage, severe burns, dehydration |
| **Cardiogenic** | ↑ (congestion) | ↓ | ↑ (compensatory) | ↓ | Massive MI, myocarditis, severe valve failure |
| **Obstructive** | ↑ (tamponade/PE/tension PTX) | ↓ | ↑ (compensatory) | ↓ | Tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE |
| **Distributive** | ↓ or normal | ↑ (early warm) or ↓ (late) | ↓ (vasoplegia) | ↑ or normal | Septic shock, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock |

Acute haemorrhage illustrates multi-organ physiological integration in real time. Losing 15% of blood volume (Class I, ~750 mL in a 70-kg adult) triggers immediate carotid baroreceptor unloading, sympathetic tachycardia, and venoconstriction that preserve blood pressure almost completely. Between 15% and 30% loss (Class II, 750 to 1,500 mL), alpha-1 arteriolar vasoconstriction elevates diastolic blood pressure and narrows pulse pressure while heart rate climbs above 100 bpm; reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure shifts Starling equilibrium toward transcapillary refill from the interstitium, gradually diluting haematocrit over hours (explaining why an acute haemoglobin concentration checked minutes after massive bleeding can appear falsely normal—never rely on a single early normal haemoglobin to exclude active haemorrhage). Beyond 30% to 40% loss (Classes III-IV, >1,500 to 2,000 mL), sympathetic compensation saturates, systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mmHg, oliguria sets in as angiotensin II and ADH surge, tissue oxygen extraction approaches its ceiling (~70%), oxygen consumption becomes supply-dependent (below critical DO2), and lactic acidosis deepens rapidly.

In neurogenic shock following high thoracic or cervical spinal cord injury (above T6), interruption of descending sympathetic vasomotor pathways abolishes both arteriolar tone and cardiac accelerator input while leaving vagal parasympathetic outflow intact—producing the unique triad of hypotension, warm flushed extremities (low SVR), and paradoxical bradycardia rather than compensatory tachycardia. In anaphylactic shock, IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation unleashes histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes causing simultaneous profound vasodilation, bronchospasm, and massive capillary leak; intramuscular epinephrine (0.3 to 0.5 mg of 1:1,000 in the anterolateral thigh) is the immediate first-line life-saving treatment, never delayed for antihistamines or corticosteroids.

Across cardiopulmonary and renal physiology, every compensatory reflex carries a ceiling and a cost. Sympathetic tachycardia sustains cardiac output until shortened diastole starves coronary perfusion; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction optimises local V/Q matching until global hypoxia causes right ventricular failure; RAAS activation defends intravascular volume until sodium retention floods alveoli; and renal bicarbonate retention buffers chronic hypercapnia until abrupt mechanical hyperventilation unmasks severe post-hypercapnic alkalosis. Clinical mastery rests on recognising which compensatory mechanism is active, measuring the exact physiological threshold at stake, and intervening without overturning the patient's remaining homeostatic reserve.

## 11. Regional Circulations: Coronary, Cerebral, Hepatic-Portal, and Cutaneous Beds

Regional vascular beds tailor blood flow tightly to organ-specific priorities, creating dramatic contrasts in basal extraction, autonomic responsiveness, and autoregulatory bounds. The myocardium operates near maximal oxygen extraction even at basal heart rates, consuming roughly 8 to 10 mL of oxygen per 100 grams of tissue per minute and returning coronary sinus blood with an oxygen saturation near 30%. Because mechanical compression during systole collapses subendocardial vessels across the left ventricular wall, more than 75% to 80% of left coronary arterial inflow takes place during diastole; the right ventricle, operating against far lower systolic pressures, receives blood throughout both systole and diastole. Metabolic vasodilators—chiefly adenosine formed from ATP breakdown, alongside nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and hyperpolarising KATP channel opening—override alpha-1 sympathetic vasoconstriction whenever myocardial workload climbs. In practical clinical terms, beta-blockers protect ischaemic myocardium not by dilating epicardial arteries directly, but by slowing heart rate to lengthen diastole while trimming wall tension and contractility.

Cerebral perfusion receives roughly 750 mL/min (15% of cardiac output, or ~50 mL per 100 g of brain tissue per minute), tightly buffered by myogenic autoregulation across mean arterial pressures from 60 to 150 mmHg in normotensive adults. In longstanding untreated hypertension, the entire autoregulatory plateau shifts rightward, meaning an abrupt drop in MAP to 70 mmHg—normally comfortable—can trigger watershed ischaemia in a chronically hypertensive patient. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure (or central venous pressure, whichever is higher): CPP = MAP - ICP. Because the adult skull is a rigid vault, the Monro-Kellie doctrine dictates that the sum of brain parenchyma, cerebrospinal fluid, and intracranial blood volume stays fixed; once buffering displacement of CSF and venous blood is exhausted, intracranial compliance plummets and tiny volume additions drive explosive rises in ICP. Carbon dioxide exerts rapid vasodilatory control across cerebral arterioles through extracellular H+ shifts in the perivascular CSF space, raising cerebral blood flow roughly 1 to 2 mL/100 g/min for every 1 mmHg increase in PaCO2 between 20 and 80 mmHg, whereas arterial PaO2 scarcely alters cerebral flow until hypoxia drops PaO2 below 50 mmHg.

The hepatic circulation is unique in receiving a dual blood supply totalling approximately 1,500 mL/min (25% to 30% of cardiac output): roughly 75% arrives as partially deoxygenated, nutrient-rich venous blood via the portal vein at low pressure (7 to 10 mmHg), while the remaining 25% enters via the hepatic artery at systemic arterial pressure and supplies roughly half of the liver's oxygen. Through the hepatic arterial buffer response—mediated largely by local adenosine washout within the space of Mall—a fall in portal venous inflow triggers compensatory hepatic arterial vasodilation to defend total hepatic perfusion, although the converse does not occur when hepatic arterial flow drops. Hepatic sinusoids are lined by fenestrated endothelium lacking a continuous basement membrane, giving them a reflection coefficient close to zero so plasma proteins equilibrate freely with the space of Disse and hepatic lymph carries nearly the same albumin concentration as plasma. When sinusoidal pressure climbs in cirrhosis or right heart failure, enormous volumes of protein-rich lymph weep from the liver capsule into the peritoneal cavity, combining with splanchnic nitric-oxide-mediated arterial vasodilation and secondary RAAS activation to produce refractory ascites.

Cutaneous blood flow serves thermoregulation rather than local metabolic demand, varying over a hundred-fold range from less than 50 mL/min during severe cold exposure to more than 3,000 mL/min during intense heat stress. Sympathetic adrenergic vasoconstrictor fibres innervate arteriovenous anastomoses in acral skin (palms, soles, ears, nose), whereas active vasodilation across non-acral trunk and limb skin depends on sympathetic cholinergic fibres co-releasing acetylcholine and vasodilatory peptides such as VIP alongside local nitric oxide synthesis. During haemorrhagic shock, hypothalamic and medullary reflexes clamp cutaneous vessels shut to redirect blood centrally, producing cool, clammy, mottled skin with delayed capillary refill time (>3 seconds)—a rapid, zero-cost bedside marker of peripheral hypoperfusion.

Skeletal muscle demonstrates the widest dynamic metabolic range in the body, transitioning from roughly 3 to 4 mL/100 g/min at rest (when sympathetic alpha-1 tone predominates) up to 80 to 100 mL/100 g/min during maximal aerobic effort. During vigorous contraction, accumulating local K+, adenosine, H+, lactate, and osmolarity override central sympathetic vasoconstriction—a phenomenon termed functional sympatholysis—ensuring active muscle fibres stay well perfused even as systemic sympathetic outflow constricts inactive muscles, kidneys, and splanchnic viscera to preserve arterial pressure.

## 12. Gastrointestinal Secretory, Absorptive, and Motility Integration

Gastrointestinal physiology coordinates motility, secretion, digestion, and absorption across roughly 7 to 9 litres of fluid entering the digestive tract daily (about 2 litres ingested plus 7 litres of salivary, gastric, biliary, pancreatic, and intestinal secretions), of which the small intestine reabsorbs roughly 80% to 85% and the colon recovers most of the remainder, leaving only 100 to 200 mL in normal stool. Smooth muscle along the gut wall generates spontaneous rhythmic slow waves paced by interstitial cells of Cajal (3 cycles/min in the stomach, 12/min in the duodenum, and 8 to 9/min in the ileum); action potentials and forceful contractions fire only when excitatory neural or hormonal input pushes slow waves past threshold. Intrinsic enteric neural plexuses—the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus coordinating longitudinal and circular peristalsis and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus regulating mucosal blood flow and epithelial secretion—can drive complete local peristaltic reflexes even without central autonomic input, while parasympathetic vagal and pelvic nerves amplify motility and secretion and sympathetic splanchnic nerves inhibit them while contracting sphincters.

Gastric acid secretion by parietal cells in the oxyntic fundus and body illustrates convergent neuroendocrine signalling onto the apical H+/K+-ATPase proton pump. Acetylcholine (vagal M3 receptor via Gq/Ca2+), gastrin (secreted by antral G cells onto CCK-B receptors via Gq/Ca2+ and indirectly stimulating enterochromaffin-like cells), and histamine (paracrine release from ECL cells acting on H2 receptors via Gs/cAMP) act synergistically so blocking H2 receptors dampens responses to all three stimuli, whereas proton pump inhibitors irreversibly covalently inactivate H+/K+-ATPase to abolish acid secretion regardless of upstream trigger. Conversely, luminal pH below 3.0 stimulates antral D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits both G cells and ECL cells via Gi signalling, while duodenal fat, acid, and hyperosmolarity trigger secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK), and GIP to brake gastric emptying and acid output. Parietal cells simultaneously secrete intrinsic factor required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum; severe autoimmune gastritis or total gastrectomy therefore mandates parenteral or high-dose replacement to prevent megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

Exocrine pancreatic secretion delivers both enzyme-rich acinar fluid (stimulated primarily by CCK in response to duodenal fatty acids and amino acids, and by vagal reflexes) and bicarbonate-rich ductal fluid (stimulated by secretin in response to duodenal acid, neutralising gastric chyme to pH 7 to 8 so pancreatic lipase and proteases operate optimally). Pancreatic proteases—trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, and proelastase—leave the pancreas strictly as inactive zymogens until duodenal brush-border enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin, which then autocatalytically activates the remaining cascade; premature intrapancreatic activation overwhelms pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor and triggers acute autodigestive pancreatitis. Bile salts synthesized from cholesterol in hepatocytes, conjugated with glycine or taurine to lower pKa and remain ionised at intestinal pH, form mixed micelles that solubilise dietary triglycerides, monoglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K across the unstirred water layer. More than 95% of secreted bile salts are actively reclaimed in the terminal ileum via apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporters (ASBT) and returned through the portal vein in the enterohepatic circulation; extensive ileal resection depletes the bile-salt pool, causes fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea, increases colonic oxalate absorption (leading to calcium oxalate kidney stones), and triggers bile-acid diarrhoea.

Intestinal water and electrolyte transport depends on electrogenic sodium-coupled cotransport in the small intestine (SGLT1 importing 2 Na+ with 1 glucose or galactose, driving passive paracellular water absorption—the physiological foundation of oral rehydration therapy even during cholera toxin-driven CFTR chloride secretion) and aldosterone-sensitive ENaC reabsorption in the distal colon. Secretory diarrhoea driven by cAMP (cholera, VIPoma) or cGMP (enterotoxigenic E. coli heat-stable toxin) persists during fasting with a low stool osmotic gap (<50 mOsm/kg), whereas osmotic diarrhoea (lactose intolerance, magnesium salts, polyethylene glycol) resolves promptly upon fasting and exhibits a wide stool osmotic gap (>100 to 125 mOsm/kg).

## 13. Endocrine Homeostasis: Glucose, Calcium-Phosphate, and Adrenal-Thyroid Axes

Endocrine control loops maintain plasma substrate concentrations, mineral balance, and basal metabolic rate across hours to weeks through closed-loop negative feedback. Pancreatic islet cells coordinate fuel partitioning between fed and fasted states. In beta cells, glucose enters via insulin-independent GLUT2 transporters, undergoes phosphorylation by glucokinase (the rate-limiting glucose sensor), and drives oxidative phosphorylation to elevate the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio; rising ATP closes KATP channels, depolarising the beta-cell membrane, opening voltage-gated calcium channels, and triggering exocytosis of equimolar insulin and C-peptide. Insulin binds receptor tyrosine kinases to activate PI3K/Akt and MAPK pathways, translocating GLUT4 vesicles to the plasma membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, stimulating hepatic and muscular glycogen synthesis, promoting lipogenesis while halting hormone-sensitive lipase, and driving Na+/K+-ATPase-mediated potassium uptake into cells. Notably, brain, erythrocytes, renal tubules, intestinal mucosa, and hepatocytes do not depend on insulin for basal glucose entry. During fasting or stress, alpha-cell glucagon (via Gs/cAMP), adrenal epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone mobilise hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ketogenesis; absolute insulin deficiency paired with unrestrained counter-regulatory hormone excess drives diabetic ketoacidosis (hyperglycaemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis from beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, osmotic diuresis, and total-body potassium depletion despite a normal or elevated initial serum potassium).

Calcium and phosphate homeostasis relies on coordinated actions of parathyroid hormone (PTH), active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, calcitriol), fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), and calcitonin across bone, kidney, and gut. Roughly 45% to 50% of total serum calcium circulates in the physiologically active ionised form (normal 1.15 to 1.30 mmol/L), 40% binds negatively charged plasma proteins (chiefly albumin), and 10% complexes with anions such as citrate, phosphate, and bicarbonate. Because hydrogen ions compete with calcium for negative binding sites on albumin, acute acidaemia displaces calcium from albumin and raises ionised calcium, whereas acute alkalaemia (such as hyperventilation during anxiety) increases albumin binding and drops ionised calcium, precipitating perioral paraesthesias, carpopedal spasm, and Chvostek or Trousseau signs despite an unchanged total serum calcium. Chief cells of the parathyroid glands monitor free ionised calcium via the G-protein-coupled calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR): low ionised calcium triggers rapid PTH secretion, which raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate by stimulating osteoblast-mediated RANKL signalling to osteoclasts (net bone resorption), enhancing distal tubular TRPV5 calcium reabsorption, blocking proximal NaPi-IIa/c phosphate reabsorption, and inducing renal proximal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to convert 25-OH-vitamin D into calcitriol. Calcitriol subsequently boosts intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate. Severe hypomagnesaemia (<1.0 mg/dL) paradoxically suppresses PTH release and induces end-organ PTH resistance, rendering hypocalcaemia refractory until serum magnesium is corrected first.

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis governs stress adaptation, vascular catecholamine sensitivity, and substrate availability. Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) drives anterior pituitary corticotrophs to cleave pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) into ACTH, beta-endorphin, and alpha-MSH (explaining mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency when loss of cortisol negative feedback surges POMC synthesis, absent in secondary pituitary insufficiency). Zona fasciculata cortisol diffuses across cell membranes to bind cytosolic glucocorticoid receptors, suppressing phospholipase A2 and NF-κB-driven cytokines, upregulating vascular alpha-1 adrenergic receptor expression to preserve vasopressor responsiveness, promoting hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral proteolysis, and demarginating neutrophils into circulating blood while reducing circulating eosinophils and lymphocytes. Zona glomerulosa aldosterone secretion responds primarily to angiotensin II and rising serum potassium rather than ACTH, which is why secondary adrenal insufficiency spares mineralocorticoid tone and rarely causes severe hyperkalaemia, whereas primary adrenal destruction (Addison disease) produces combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Thyroid hormones set basal cellular metabolic rate, thermogenesis, and beta-adrenergic receptor density across tissues. Follicular cells trap iodide via the sodium-iodide symporter, oxidise and organify iodide onto thyroglobulin tyrosines via thyroid peroxidase (inhibited by methimazole and propylthiouracil), and couple MIT and DIT into T4 (major secreted prohormone, half-life ~7 days) and T3 (biologically active hormone with ten-fold higher nuclear receptor affinity, half-life ~1 day, generated mostly by peripheral 5'-deiodinase in liver and kidney). Thyroid hormone upregulates Na+/K+-ATPase synthesis (increasing oxygen consumption and heat production), increases cardiac beta-1 receptor expression and SERCA2a transcription (producing sinus tachycardia, widened pulse pressure, and high-output heart failure in thyrotoxicosis), and accelerates LDL receptor expression (explaining hypercholesterolaemia in hypothyroidism).

## 14. Thermoregulation, Perioperative Stress Response, and Physiological Reserve

Core body temperature is regulated tightly near 37.0 °C (interthreshold range typically 36.8 to 37.2 °C) by the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus, integrating central core thermoreceptors (spinal cord, viscera, great vessels) with peripheral cutaneous cold and warm sensors. Autonomic defences against cold begin with cutaneous vasoconstriction and non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (critical in neonates who lack effective shivering), followed at roughly 1 °C lower core temperature by involuntary skeletal muscle shivering—which can double or triple whole-body oxygen consumption and precipitate myocardial ischaemia in patients with coronary artery disease. Defences against heat deploy active cutaneous vasodilation and eccrine sweating; evaporation of sweat removes roughly 580 kcal per litre of fluid evaporated and represents the sole effective heat-loss pathway when ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature, though evaporative cooling collapses in 100% relative humidity.

General anaesthesia and neuraxial blockade profoundly impair hypothalamic thermoregulation by widening the interthreshold range from roughly 0.2 °C up to 4.0 °C, abolishing vasoconstriction and shivering across mild hypothermia. Within the first hour after induction of general anaesthesia, core temperature drops 1.0 to 1.5 °C predominantly through internal core-to-peripheral redistribution of heat along dilated cutaneous beds rather than immediate net heat loss to the operating room; thereafter, radiation (roughly 40% to 60% of net loss), convection, evaporation from open surgical cavities, and conduction continue cooling the patient unless active forced-air warming and warmed intravenous fluids are deployed. Even mild perioperative hypothermia (<36.0 °C) impairs platelet function and coagulation cascade enzyme kinetics (increasing surgical blood loss and transfusion requirements), triples surgical-site infection risk through subcutaneous vasoconstriction and impaired neutrophil oxidative killing, prolongs metabolism of neuromuscular blockers and volatile agents, and provokes postoperative shivering surges in VO2 and catecholamines.

Major surgical trauma or critical illness activates a stereotyped neuroendocrine and inflammatory stress response designed originally for short-term survival after injury. Afferent nociceptive fibres from the surgical site stimulate hypothalamic release of CRH, ADH, and sympathetic outflow, driving hyperglycaemia via insulin resistance and hepatic gluconeogenesis, salt and water retention via aldosterone and ADH (producing physiologic postoperative oliguria that must not be misread automatically as hypovolaemia when haemodynamics and perfusion markers are normal), and catabolic skeletal muscle proteolysis supplying amino acids for hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis (C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, complement). Regional analgesia such as thoracic epidural blockade attenuates afferent nociceptive traffic, blunts catecholamine surges, reduces postoperative ileus, and improves pulmonary mechanics after upper abdominal or thoracic surgery, illustrating how targeted modulation of integrated physiology protects organ reserve across the perioperative continuum.

Ageing gradually narrows physiological reserve across every organ system discussed in this chapter without necessarily altering resting baseline numbers. In the cardiovascular system, arterial stiffening elevates systolic blood pressure and pulse pressure while declining beta-adrenergic receptor responsiveness limits maximal exercise heart rate (approximated by 220 minus age) and forces older ventricles to rely more heavily on Frank-Starling preload augmentation and atrial kick—explaining why new-onset atrial fibrillation or mild dehydration precipitates abrupt decompensation in elderly patients. In the respiratory system, loss of parenchymal elastic recoil increases closing capacity until small airways collapse during normal tidal breathing in the supine position (typically past age 65), widening the A-a gradient and speeding arterial desaturation during apnoea or induction of anaesthesia. In the kidney, nephron mass and GFR decline progressively by roughly 0.8 to 1.0 mL/min/year past age 40, while reduced lean muscle mass keeps serum creatinine deceptively normal despite substantially diminished creatinine clearance—demanding weight- and age-adjusted dosing for renally cleared drugs. Recognising the boundary between resting equilibrium and depleted reserve ties together membrane electrophysiology, pressure-volume mechanics, gas exchange, nephron transport, and endocrine feedback into a unified clinical framework.
